newsitem.title: CHILE: COPPER - Chile smelters move clean-up plans ahead.
newsitem.headline: COPPER - Chile smelters move clean-up plans ahead.

text.p: The El Teniente division of Chilean state copper company Codelco has started building work on a $70 million sulphuric acid plant, in the first step of clean up at its dirty Caletones smelter, said officials.

It will be the first of three plants the pit plans to build over the next 12 years under an anti-pollution program Codelco has submitted to environmental authority Conama for approval, said Mario Barrera of the division's environment control unit.

"We are optimistic Conama will approve the plan, although they may order the plants to be built more rapidly," he said. The plant, which converts sulphur dioxide gas into acid, is part of a $600 million drive by Codelco to clean up its three copper smelters, which are among the country's worst industrial polluters.
The acid will be sold to other mines which spray it over mineral to extract copper in a much cleaner process known as heap-leaching which bypasses the traditional concentrator and smelter.

An anti-contamination plan is already underway at the giant Chuquicamata pit -- whose smoky fumes can been seen from miles away -- with a similar program expected to be started soon at the much smaller Salvador mine.
Also involved is another state mining company, Enami, which will spend over $100 million by the end of the decade in cutting emissions at its Ventanas and Paipote plants.
The programs, most of which will be completed by 1999, follow a government decree in 1992 which slashes emissions of sulphur dioxide, toxic particles and arsenic.

Regulations ordering plants to cut sulphur dioxide pollution by up to 95 percent are already in force and are on a par with international standards, said professor Gustavo Lagos of the mining department at Santiago's Catholic University.
But rules governing emissions of arsenic, which have been under discussion for several years, have yet to be agreed.

The problem is that mineral in the northern Atacama Desert, at the heart of Chile's mining industry, is so high in arsenic that arsenic levels in the air from dust already exceed international standards, said Lagos.
"It is difficult to rule on arsenic emissions as the basic level in areas surrounding many smelters is already above international norms," he said.
Arsenic is particularly problematic for Chuquicamata, Paipote and the privately run Refimet complex, he said. --Santiago newsroom, 562-699-5595x212
